  1541      OPM responds to comments regarding specific sections of this rule 
  1542  below.
  1543  
  1544  A. Part 351, Subpart B: Changes in Definitions, Coverage, Use of 
  1545  Regulations, and Agency Responsibilities
  1546  
  1547  1. Erosion of Duties Reclassifications
  1548      OPM is modifying Sec.  351.201(a)(2) to remove from the list of 
  1549  actions that require agencies to use RIF procedures reclassification of 
  1550  an employee's position due to erosion of duties if the action would 
  1551  take effect after an agency had formally announced a RIF in the 
  1552  employee's competitive area and the RIF would take effect within 180 
  1553  days.
  1554      Commenter 0532 argued that OPM has not justified removing erosion-
  1555  of-duties reclassifications from the actions requiring RIF procedures. 
  1556  OPM disagrees.
  1557      The proposed rule explains the history of the erosion-of-duties 
  1558  provision. In 1986, OPM generally removed erosion-of-duties 
  1559  reclassifications from the categories of actions subject to RIF 
  1560  procedures, but retained a narrow RIF-procedure requirement for 
  1561  reclassifications occurring after announcement of a RIF and within 180 
  1562  days of the RIF effective date. OPM is now removing that narrow 
  1563  procedural trigger because it is unreasonable and impracticable to 
  1564  require agencies to build a retention register for such 
  1565  reclassifications, and OPM is not aware of any agency actually 
  1566  executing an erosion-of-duties reclassification action using RIF 
  1567  procedures since the 1986 revision.
  1568      Commenter 0037 argued that the ``erosion of duties'' changes could 
  1569  be used to constructively demote disfavored employees. OPM disagrees. 
  1570  Erosion of duties reclassifications have generally been excluded from 
  1571  RIF procedures since 1986, except in the narrow circumstance where the 
  1572  reclassification will take effect after an agency has formally 
  1573  announced a RIF in the employee's competitive area that will take 
  1574  effect within 180 days. This rule directly addresses concerns that 
  1575  erosion-of-duties reclassifications could be used to undermine the RIF 
  1576  retention order. Rather than requiring a full RIF process for erosion-
  1577  of-duties reclassifications, this rule will bar agencies from 
  1578  undertaking an erosion-of-duties reclassification between the formal 
  1579  announcement and completion of a RIF if the action would adversely 
  1580  affect an employee's retention standing in the RIF. This is a more 
  1581  direct and administrable safeguard than the current rule. Notably, 
  1582  commenters 0037 and 0532 do not identify any concrete instance in which 
  1583  the existing erosion-of-duties RIF trigger has been necessary to 
  1584  protect employees, nor do
  1585  
  1586  [[Page 49191]]
  1587  
  1588  commenters 0037 or 0532 explain why the proposed anti-manipulation 
  1589  prohibition would be inadequate.
  1590      Instead, OPM agrees with Commenter 0720, a Federal agency, that the 
  1591  current erosion-of-duties provision is outdated, and OPM's approach in 
  1592  this rule ``reduces unnecessary confusion and risk while preserving 
  1593  safeguards against improper alterations to retention outcomes.''
  1594  2. Employees Excluded From RIF Competition
  1595      This rule modifies the definition of the term Competing employee in 
  1596  Sec.  351.203 to mean an employee in the competitive service tenure 
  1597  group or the excepted service tenure group. It also adds a definition 
  1598  of Competitive service tenure group to mean all employees within 
  1599  competitive service tenure subgroups I and II; that is, all employees 
  1600  in the competitive service who, as of the date of the RIF notice, are 
  1601  not serving an initial probationary period or a temporary appointment 
  1602  of 1 year or less under subpart D of 5 CFR part 316. This rule defines 
  1603  the Excepted service tenure group as all employees within excepted 
  1604  service tenure subgroups I and II; that is, all excepted service 
  1605  appointees serving in a career position (that is, not in Schedule C or 
  1606  G) who, as of the date of the RIF notice, are not serving a trial 
  1607  period or in a temporary or time-limited appointment of 1 year or less.
  1608      OPM is also adding definitions of initial probationary period and 
  1609  trial period to Sec.  351.203. With respect to these provisions, OPM 
  1610  notes that a supervisory or managerial employee with career tenure who 
  1611  is only on probation with respect to those supervisory or managerial 
  1612  functions (i.e., is entitled to be returned to a nonsupervisory or non-
  1613  managerial position rather than being subject to removal under 5 CFR 
  1614  part 315, subpart I) would be included in the RIF in the supervisory or 
  1615  managerial position, and would not be subject to the exclusion from RIF 
  1616  procedures applicable to individuals serving an initial probationary 
  1617  period under 5 CFR 11.2. Further, an employee who is serving both an 
  1618  initial probationary period and a supervisory probationary period 
  1619  simultaneously is exempt from RIF procedures.
  1620      In the proposed rule, OPM proposed to add a Sec.  351.202(d) that 
  1621  lists categories of employees excluded from RIF retention procedures, 
  1622  as they fall outside the definition of ``competing employees'' under 5 
  1623  U.S.C. 3502(a). Under OPM's definition of ``competing employees,'' 
  1624  employees in the competitive service who are serving an initial 
  1625  probationary period would be excluded from RIF procedures, as would 
  1626  employees in the excepted service who are serving a trial period. In 
  1627  addition, competitive and excepted service employees who are serving 
  1628  temporary or time-limited appointments of 1 year or less would be 
  1629  excluded from RIF competition, as would Schedule C and Schedule G 
  1630  employees.
  1631      In this final rule, OPM is revising the wording of Sec.  
  1632  351.202(d). The revised wording narrows Sec.  351.202(d) from a broad 
  1633  statement that certain employees are excluded from part 351 altogether 
  1634  to a more precise statement that they are not ``competing employees'' 
  1635  for RIF purposes. The final rule clarifies the consequences of this 
  1636  classification: an agency may retain such an employee while releasing a 
  1637  competing employee, and may furlough, separate, demote, or reassign 
  1638  such an employee for a reason described in Sec.  351.201(a)(2) (lack of 
  1639  work, shortage of funds, insufficient personnel ceiling, 
  1640  reorganization, or the exercise of reemployment rights or restoration 
  1641  rights) without determining the employee's retention standing under 
  1642  subparts D and E, applying the order-of-release provisions in subpart 
  1643  F, or providing assignment rights under subpart G, provided the action 
  1644  is otherwise consistent with the terms of the employee's appointment 
  1645  and applicable law. Further, the revised text clarifies that these 
  1646  excluded employees are still subject to the notice provisions of Sec.  
  1647  351.801 where they are furloughed for more than 30 days, separated, 
  1648  demoted, or reassigned for the reasons described in Sec.  
  1649  351.201(a)(2), and the action is not merely the expiration of a 
  1650  temporary or time-limited appointment according to its terms. Under 
  1651  such circumstances the agency must provide the employee a modified 
  1652  written notice that includes the action to be taken, the reasons for 
  1653  the action, and its effective date; a link to 5 CFR part 351 and access 
  1654  to the agency's records pertinent to the reduction in force being 
  1655  taken; information on reemployment rights; and any appeal rights.
  1656      In addition, the final rule makes other wording changes to Sec.  
  1657  351.202(d). It revises the Schedule C and Schedule G language by 
  1658  referring to employees ``serving under'' those appointments and removes 
  1659  a proposed reference to term appointments under part 316 subpart C, 
  1660  making clear that the competitive-service temporary-appointment 
  1661  exclusion is limited to temporary appointments of 1 year or less under 
  1662  part 316 subpart D.
  1663      Commenter 0719, a Federal agency, supported the proposed changes 
  1664  excluding initial probationary period and trial period employees from 
  1665  RIF competition, noting that the current RIF rules demand that 
  1666  probationary and trial period employees be released first in a RIF. 
  1667  Commenter 0719 noted that this results in ``the loss of high potential 
  1668  individuals essential for long term succession planning and mission 
  1669  continuity.'' The agency noted that ``[r]emoving these groups from RIF 
  1670  competition will allow [it] greater flexibility to retain high 
  1671  potential early career employees even in constrained budget 
  1672  conditions.'' Commenter 0687 noted that termination of probationary 
  1673  employees as part of workforce reshaping activities can ``weaken[] 
  1674  early career pipelines'' and result in the loss of some of the agency's 
  1675  ``best talent.'' OPM agrees.
  1676      Commenter 0678 claimed that these exclusions would mean that the 
  1677  RIF regulations would no longer provide a comprehensive system to 
  1678  govern workforce reductions, while Commenter 0684 argued that this 
  1679  change would conflict with 5 U.S.C. 3501(b)'s broad coverage provision. 
  1680  OPM disagrees. OPM has long used its authority under 5 U.S.C. 3502 to 
  1681  define the otherwise-undefined statutory term ``competing employees'' 
  1682  subject to RIF competition to exclude certain groups of employees from 
  1683  RIF retention procedures. For example, in its regulations at 5 CFR 
  1684  316.911, OPM recognizes that employees ``whose initial appointment [is] 
  1685  for a period of 1 year or less are not assigned a tenure group and do 
  1686  not compete with other employees in a RIF.'' In its regulations at 5 
  1687  CFR 353.209, OPM stated that an employee performing duty with the 
  1688  uniformed services ``is not a `competing employee' under'' the RIF 
  1689  regulations. And OPM's regulations at 5 CFR 351.705 have long provided 
  1690  that an agency may, but is not required to, provide assignment rights 
  1691  to excepted service employees.
  1692      Related statutory provisions, and the broader history of 
  1693  probationary and trial periods in the Federal service, support OPM's 
  1694  determination that probationary and trial period employees should not 
  1695  be considered ``competing employees'' for purposes of 5 U.S.C. 3502. 
  1696  The phrase ``competing employee'' in 5 U.S.C. 3502 must be read against 
  1697  a long background tracing to the Pendleton Act of 1883 whereby Congress 
  1698  has consistently and deliberately maintained a distinction between 
  1699  employees whose appointments have become final and employees still 
  1700  serving a probationary or trial period. This distinction reflects a 
  1701  longstanding congressional and regulatory judgment that competitive 
  1702  selection alone is not the final test of fitness for Federal
  1703  
  1704  [[Page 49192]]
  1705  
  1706  service. Rather, an initial period of actual service has always served 
  1707  as the Government's final opportunity to determine whether an employee 
  1708  should receive the full procedural protections associated with 
  1709  continuing Federal employment.
  1710      The Pendleton Act (22 Stat. 403) required that the ``there shall be 
  1711  a period of probation before any absolute appointment or employment 
  1712  aforesaid.'' That statutory formulation indicates that Congress did not 
  1713  treat appointment and final appointment as the same event. It preserved 
  1714  a two-step process--competitive appointment first, with final 
  1715  appointment only after satisfactory completion of probation.
  1716      In its first annual report in 1884, the Civil Service Commission 
  1717  characterized the probationary period as lasting ``six months before 
  1718  any absolute appointment can be made. At the end of this time the 
  1719  appointee goes out of the service unless then reappointed.'' \7\ Two 
  1720  years later, the Commission wrote in its third annual report that 
  1721  ``doing the public work is precisely what the Merit System provides. If 
  1722  at its termination the appointing officer is not . . . willing to make 
  1723  an unconditional appointment, the probationer is . . . absolutely out 
  1724  of the service without any action on the part of the Government.'' \8\
  1725  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1726  
  1727      \7\ First Annual Report of the United States Civil Service 
  1728  Commission to the President (1884), p. 29, https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=nnc1.cu09006737&seq=9.
  1729      \8\ Third Annual Report of the United States Civil Service 
  1730  Commission to the President (1886), p. 36, https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=njp.32101073361022&seq=40.
  1731  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1732  
  1733      With the enactment of the Lloyd-La Follette Act of 1912, Congress 
  1734  created the first legislative codification of protection against 
  1735  removal for civil servants. The Act established ``[t]hat no person in 
  1736  the classified civil service of the United States shall be removed 
  1737  therefrom except for such cause as will promote the efficiency of said 
  1738  service.'' \9\ The Act also imposed certain procedural requirements on 
  1739  removals including advance notice and an opportunity to respond in 
  1740  writing. However, Congress did not establish employment protections for 
  1741  probationary employees, and has maintained this exclusion through every 
  1742  subsequent recodification of the civil service laws.
  1743  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1744  
  1745      \9\ The Lloyd-La Follette Act, 37 Stat. 555 (1912), as amended, 
  1746  62 Stat. 354 (1948), 5 U.S.C.A. 652(a).
  1747  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1748  
  1749      Congress legislated against this backdrop in using the term 
  1750  ``competing employees'' in the Veterans' Preference Act of 1944 \10\--
  1751  the direct legislative predecessor of 5 U.S.C. 3502. The Veterans' 
  1752  Preference Act of 1944 did not define ``competing employees'' to 
  1753  include all individuals serving in Federal positions. Instead, Section 
  1754  12 of that Act provided that, in a reduction in personnel, ``competing 
  1755  employees'' would be released in accordance with Civil Service 
  1756  Commission regulations giving due effect to the statutory retention 
  1757  factors. Congress thus left the identification of the competitive group 
  1758  to regulation.
  1759  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1760  
  1761      \10\ Public Law 78-359, 58 Stat. 387 (codified, as amended in 
  1762  part, at 5 U.S.C. 3309-3320).
  1763  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1764  
  1765      This is particularly significant because, in Section 14, the 
  1766  Veterans' Preference Act expanded civil service protections to 
  1767  preference eligible Federal employees, but it explicitly excluded 
  1768  probationers, limiting its protections to a ``permanent or indefinite 
  1769  preference eligible, who has completed a probationary or trial 
  1770  period.'' Section 12 and section 14 were enacted in the same statute. 
  1771  If Congress believed probationary and trial-period employees 
  1772  necessarily had to be treated the same as final appointees for all 
  1773  retention-related purposes, it would be odd for Congress, two sections 
  1774  later, to condition major procedural protections on completion of 
  1775  probationary or trial service. The better reading is that the 1944 Act 
  1776  preserved a two-step civil-service model: an employee could enter 
  1777  Federal service and receive whatever preference rights the statute and 
  1778  regulations afforded, but the employee did not necessarily become part 
  1779  of the competitive retention workforce before completing the 
  1780  probationary or trial period.
  1781      The statutory text of 5 U.S.C. 3502(a) therefore does not compel 
  1782  OPM to include employees serving an initial probationary or trial 
  1783  period in RIF competition; rather, it permits OPM to determine by 
  1784  regulation that such employees are not ``competing employees'' for 
  1785  purposes of retention registers and order of release, while preserving 
  1786  any independently applicable statutory or regulatory protections.\11\
  1787  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1788  
  1789      \11\ Commenter 0684 points to Fathauer v. United States, 566 
  1790  F.3d 1352 (Fed. Cir. 2009), but that case is inapposite. Here, OPM 
  1791  is not defining ``employee'' in 5 U.S.C. 3501(b) to nullify 
  1792  statutory coverage. Instead, it is defining the narrower, undefined 
  1793  term ``competing employee'' in section 3502(a), a term Congress 
  1794  expressly left for implementation through OPM regulations.
  1795  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1796  
  1797      The current 5 U.S.C. 7511 codifies the longstanding exclusion of 
  1798  probationary and trial period employees from the adverse-action 
  1799  definition of ``employee.'' Under 5 U.S.C. 7511, an ``employee'' in the 
  1800  competitive service or excepted service generally means an individual 
  1801  who is not serving a probationary or trial period under an initial 
  1802  appointment or who has completed one year of current continuous service 
  1803  under other than a temporary appointment limited to one year or less.
  1804      Courts interpreting section 7511 and related CSRA provisions have 
  1805  repeatedly recognized that Congress intended agencies to retain 
  1806  substantial flexibility over probationary and trial-period employees. 
  1807  In Department of Justice v. FLRA, the D.C. Circuit relied on the CSRA's 
  1808  structure and legislative history in concluding that probationary 
  1809  employees could not obtain through negotiated grievance procedures the 
  1810  kind of review Congress deliberately withheld from them in chapter 
  1811  75.\12\ 709 F.2d 724, 730 (D.C. Cir. 1983). In United States v. 
  1812  Connolly, the Federal Circuit likewise treated the exclusion of 
  1813  probationary employees from chapter 75 appeal rights as a deliberate 
  1814  congressional choice, not a statutory gap for courts or agencies to 
  1815  fill.\13\ And in National Treasury Employees Union v. FLRA, the D.C. 
  1816  Circuit reaffirmed that the CSRA's treatment of probationary employees 
  1817  reflects Congress's judgment that agencies must have latitude to assess 
  1818  and separate employees who have not yet completed the testing period 
  1819  for Federal service.\14\ This history does not mean that section 7511 
  1820  directly controls chapter 35 RIF procedures. It does, however, confirm 
  1821  that OPM's treatment of probationary, trial-period, and short-term 
  1822  temporary employees in this rule is consistent with the broader civil-
  1823  service framework Congress enacted.
  1824  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1825  
  1826      \12\ See Dep't of Justice v. FLRA, 709 F.2d 724, 730 (D.C. Cir. 
  1827  1983).
  1828      \13\ See U.S. v. Connolly, 716 F.2d 882, 886 (Fed. Cir. 1983).
  1829      \14\ See Nat'l Treasury Emps. Union v. FLRA, 848 F.2d 1273, 1275 
  1830  (D.C. Cir. 1988).
  1831  ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1832  
  1833      In addition, 5 U.S.C. 3502 should be read consistent with 5 U.S.C. 
  1834  3321, which contemplates a probationary period before an appointment 
  1835  becomes final and allows the President to issue rules and regulations 
  1836  effectuating probationary periods. Current Civil Service Rule 11, 
  1837  issued by the President under Executive Order (E.O.) 14284, already 
  1838  supplies a comprehensive framework for probationary and trial-period 
  1839  employment. It requires agencies to use probationary and trial periods

  1840  to evaluate whether an employee's continuation in Federal service 
  1841  advances the public interest and expressly permits agencies to consider 
  1842  agency needs and interests, whether continued employment would advance 
  1843  agency or Government organizational goals, and whether continued
  1844  
  1845  [[Page 49193]]
  1846  
  1847  employment would advance the efficiency of the service.
  1848      Those considerations substantially overlap with the reasons 
  1849  agencies conduct RIFs, including lack of work, shortage of funds, and 
  1850  reorganization. Requiring agencies to apply full part 351 retention-
  1851  register, order-of-release, and assignment-right procedures to 
  1852  employees whose appointments have not yet become final would duplicate 
  1853  Rule 11 and could produce inconsistent outcomes. For example, Rule 11 
  1854  might support retaining a probationary employee because the employee 
  1855  has scarce skills, strong actual performance, and is needed for the 
  1856  agency's future mission. But a part 351 retention register would likely 
  1857  place the same employee low because the employee has little service 
  1858  time and may lack a rating of record. Thus, excluding probationary and 
  1859  trial period employees from the statutory definition of ``competing 
  1860  employees'' in 5 U.S.C. 3502(a) eliminates duplication and makes sense 
  1861  of the overall statutory scheme.
  1862      With respect to temporary employees, OPM's regulations at 5 CFR 
  1863  part 316, subpart D make clear that such appointments are only 
  1864  appropriate to meet short-term needs, including ``for such reasons as 
  1865  abolishment, reorganization, or contracting of the function, 
  1866  anticipated reduction in funding, or completion of a specific project 
  1867  or peak workload.'' 5 CFR 316.401(a)(2). Further, ``[t]he supervisor of 
  1868  each position filled by temporary appointment must certify that the 
  1869  employment need is truly temporary and that the proposed appointment 
  1870  meets the regulatory time limits.'' Id. 316.401(b). Thus, these 
  1871  regulations indicate that temporary employees do not have a reasonable 
  1872  expectation of long-term employment and thus should not be considered 
  1873  ``competing employees'' for purposes of 5 U.S.C. 3502.
  1874      Further, in the final rule, OPM has clarified that the employees 
  1875  excluded from RIF competition are not entirely outside the regulatory 
  1876  scheme and must receive a notice in accordance with 5 U.S.C. 3502(d) 
  1877  when they are furloughed for more than 30 days, separated, demoted, or 
  1878  reassigned for reasons of lack of work, shortage of funds, insufficient 
  1879  personnel ceiling, reorganization, or the exercise of reemployment 
  1880  rights or restoration rights and the action is not merely the 
  1881  expiration of a temporary or time-limited appointment according to its 
  1882  terms. In addition, the regulations provide in Sec.  351.605 that all 
  1883  positions in the competitive area, including those of employees 
  1884  excluded from RIF competition under Sec.  351.202(d), must be abolished 
  1885  within 180 days for an agency to permissibly use the streamlined 
  1886  procedures of that subpart.
  1887      Commenter 0672 objected that probationary employees can be covered 
  1888  by the proposal's missing-rating rules and therefore should remain in 
  1889  RIF competition. OPM does not agree that the proposed modal-rating 
  1890  provision eliminates the need to exclude probationary and trial-period 
  1891  employees from RIF competition. The modal-rating rule is a limited 
  1892  proxy for competing employees who lack ratings in the applicable 
  1893  lookback period; it does not provide an individualized measure of 
  1894  performance for employees whose appointments have not yet been 
  1895  finalized and who often have not served long enough to receive a rating 
  1896  of record. In a performance-first RIF system, assigning retention 
  1897  standing to such employees based on the most common rating assigned to 
  1898  other employees would fail to measure the employee's own performance. 
  1899  OPM therefore reasonably treats probationary and trial-period employees 
  1900  outside the retention-register process and permits agencies to retain, 
  1901  finalize, or separate them under the rules applicable to their 
  1902  appointments, instead of the RIF rules.
  1903      Further, the modal-rating approach does not address the separate 
  1904  legal and personnel-management function of probationary and trial 
  1905  periods. Civil Service Rule 11 provides that agencies must use 
  1906  probationary and trial periods to evaluate an employee's fitness and 
  1907  whether continued employment advances the public interest; the agency 
  1908  may consider performance and conduct, agency needs, organizational 
  1909  goals, and efficiency of the service before finalizing the appointment. 
  1910  A modal RIF rating cannot replace that appointment-finalization 
  1911  judgment. It does not tell the agency whether the employee has 
  1912  demonstrated sufficient fitness, adaptability, conduct, judgment, or 
  1913  mission fit to warrant final appointment. It simply imputes a rating 
  1914  based on how other employees were rated. That is a poor fit for 
  1915  employees who are still in the government's final assessment period.
  1916      Commenters 0674 and 0680 argued that excluding temporary, 
  1917  probationary and trial period employees from RIF procedures could mean 
  1918  that certain employees still covered by RIF regulations would be 
  1919  released ahead of more junior employees, thus undermining tenure as a 
  1920  statutory retention factor. But 5 U.S.C. 3502 does not prescribe a 
  1921  strict ``last in, first out'' system. It does not define ``competing 
  1922  employees,'' does not require every employee in an agency to compete 
  1923  against every other employee, and does not require agencies to retain 
  1924  every more senior employee ahead of every less senior employee in all 
  1925  circumstances. Instead, it directed OPM to create regulations for the 
  1926  release of competing employees and to give ``due effect'' to several 
  1927  factors. ``Due effect'' does not mean controlling effect, equal effect, 
  1928  or absolute effect in every possible comparison. Nor does it mean that 
  1929  tenure must always override appointment status, performance, agency 
  1930  needs, or the threshold question whether an employee has a finalized 
  1931  appointment and belongs in RIF competition at all. OPM therefore may 
  1932  reasonably distinguish between employees who have completed the period 
  1933  necessary to obtain a finalized appointment and employees who remain in 
  1934  a temporary, probationary, or trial status.
  1935      Commenter 0115 expressed concern that excluding probationary and 
  1936  temporary employees from RIF procedures might hurt efforts to recruit 
  1937  early-career talent. However, probationary, trial period, and temporary 
  1938  employees are the most likely to be separated under the current RIF 
  1939  rules, which require agencies to place these employees at the bottom of 
  1940  the retention register due to their lack of tenure and seniority. The 
  1941  changes in this rulemaking make it much more likely that an agency will 
  1942  be able to retain these employees post-restructuring, as the decision 
  1943  to retain or separate these employees would no longer depend on their 
  1944  retention standing.
  1945      Commenter 0683 urged OPM to consider the impact of the exclusion of 
  1946  probationary employees from RIF procedures on leadership pipeline 
  1947  investments, and to recommend that agencies account for leadership 
  1948  development considerations in their workforce planning. OPM agrees that 
  1949  agencies should closely consider the impact on leadership pipelines in 
  1950  determining whether agencies should release probationary employees in a 
  1951  reduction in force. Indeed, OPM notes that the regulatory flexibility 
  1952  to exclude probationary employees from RIF procedures is essential to 
  1953  protecting investments that agencies have made in recruiting 
  1954  outstanding early career employees.
  1955      Commenters 0037 and 0678 argued that the changes remove procedural 
  1956  protections from these employees, while Commenters 0680 and 0672 
  1957  referenced past instances where probationary employees were allegedly 
  1958  subject to termination without regard to their
  1959  
  1960  [[Page 49194]]
  1961  
  1962  performance. However, probationary, trial period and temporary 
  1963  employees will continue to be protected by the Merit System Principles 
  1964  codified in 5 U.S.C. 2301, which require that Federal employees receive 
  1965  fair and equitable treatment in personnel management without regard to 
  1966  political affiliation, and that they receive protection against 
  1967  arbitrary action or coercion for partisan political purposes. In 
  1968  addition, probationary and trial period employees will also continue to 
  1969  be subject to applicable procedures under Civil Service Rule 11, while 
  1970  probationary employees would be able to appeal their terminations to 
  1971  OPM under the proposed rule ``Streamlining Probationary and Trial 
  1972  Period Appeals'' (90 FR 61070). In addition, in the final rule, OPM is 
  1973  revising Sec.  351.202(d) to note specifically that actions to retain, 
  1974  furlough, separate, demote or reassign employees excluded from RIF 
  1975  competition must be consistent with the terms of the employee's 
  1976  appointment and applicable law, and that such employees must be 
  1977  provided a modified RIF notice.
  1978      Thus, these changes will not subject probationary and trial period 
  1979  employees to arbitrary action, retaliation, or pretextual decision-
  1980  making without redress. Instead, the changes make it more likely that 
  1981  these employees could be retained post-restructuring and recognize 
  1982  relevant differences between these categories of employees and others 
  1983  (namely, their limited performance history) while maintaining the 
  1984  procedural rights appropriate to their employment.
  1985      Commenter 0685 urged that OPM adopt a presumption of retention for 
  1986  probationary employees. OPM does not adopt this suggestion, as the 
  1987  subject of probationary employment is covered comprehensively in E.O. 
  1988  14284 and Civil Service Rule 11 (5 CFR part 11), which provide clear 
  1989  processes for evaluating probationary employees. In addition, OPM notes 
  1990  that the Merit System Principles codified in 5 U.S.C. 2301 and OPM's 
  1991  parallel rulemaking regarding appeals for probationary employees 
  1992  provide further protections for this group of employees.
  1993  3. Emergency Shutdown Furloughs
  1994      OPM is modifying the definition of the term furlough in Sec.  
  1995  351.203 to exclude an emergency shutdown furlough caused by a lapse in 
  1996  congressional appropriations where the ultimate duration of the 
  1997  furlough is not known by the agency at the outset of the furlough. 
  1998  Commenters generally supported this change. Commenter 0687 noted that 
  1999  because ``Congress has subsequently guaranteed backpay to federal 
  2000  employees in a law signed by President Trump in 2019'' and thus ``all 
  2001  employees are eventually compensated by law for time they would 
  2002  otherwise be at work'' (unlike in the case of an unpaid RIF furlough), 
  2003  a RIF furlough notice should not be required in emergency shutdown 
  2004  furloughs. Commenter 0686, a Federal agency, commented that ``[t]his 
  2005  change improves efficiency and ensures employees are not subject to 
  2006  repeated, unnecessary notices when a furlough is based on a lack of 
  2007  appropriations.'' In the final rule, OPM is making a minor, non-
  2008  substantive change to remove the limitation that the length of the 
  2009  furlough must be ``dependent entirely on congressional action, rather 
  2010  than agency action'' to avoid confusion (as agencies often call 
  2011  employees back to work during government shutdowns of unknown length 
  2012  that are caused by lapses in appropriations).
  2013  4. Transfers of Function
  2014      OPM is revising Sec.  351.203 to modify the definition of transfer 
  2015  of function to adhere to the text of the applicable statute enacted by 
  2016  Congress to govern transfers of function, 5 U.S.C. 3503. That statute 
  2017  only applies to a situation ``[w]hen a function is transferred from one 
  2018  agency to another . . . .'' (emphasis added).
  2019      Commenters 0672 and 0674 argued that narrowing transfer-of-function 
  2020  procedures would weaken employee protections and allow agencies to 
  2021  evade RIF rules through internal reorganizations. OPM disagrees. This 
  2022  rule does not allow agencies to evade RIF requirements when an internal 
  2023  reorganization results in release from a competitive level for RIF 
  2024  reasons. Rather, it distinguishes between interagency transfers of 
  2025  function, where governmentwide transfer-of-function protections are 
  2026  statutorily required, and internal management realignments, where 
  2027  ordinary reassignment principles can address any resulting personnel 
  2028  actions and offer adequate protections for employees. Specifically, 
  2029  transfers and reassignments of employees in the competitive service 
  2030  within agencies will continue to be governed by 5 CFR part 335. 
  2031  Transfers and reassignments of employees within agencies in the 
  2032  excepted service will continue to be governed by 5 CFR parts 213 and 
  2033  302. Further, 5 U.S.C. 2301 requires agencies to adhere to Merit System 
  2034  Principles in personnel management, including transfers and 
  2035  reassignments of employees, and in the final rule OPM is amending Sec.  
  2036  351.204 to provide specifically that its 5 CFR part 351 regulations 
  2037  must be administered and applied consistent with all applicable laws, 
  2038  including the Merit System Principles set forth in 5 U.S.C. 2301(b).
  2039      Commenter 0719, a Federal agency, stated that ``[t]he updated 
  2040  definition for transfer of function will remove constraints that 
  2041  currently impede timely organizational adjustments,'' noting that 
  2042  existing rules result in ``administrative obstacles that slow [its] 
  2043  ability to adapt quickly to emerging needs.'' Commenter 0719 noted 
  2044  that, ``[u]nder existing regulations, even straightforward internal 
  2045  realignments can require extensive procedures, discouraging agencies 
  2046  from implementing changes that could reduce duplication, improve 
  2047  efficiency, or better align staff with mission priorities.'' OPM 
  2048  agrees.
  2049  5. Other Definitions
  2050      In this rule, OPM is providing a formal definition of ``reduction 
  2051  in force'': the release of a competing employee from his or her 
  2052  competitive level by furlough for more than 30 days, separation, or 
  2053  demotion, or reassignment requiring displacement, when the release is 
  2054  required because of lack of work; shortage of funds; insufficient 
  2055  personnel ceiling; reorganization; or the exercise of reemployment 
  2056  rights or restoration rights. OPM did not receive significant comments

  2065  when computing the performance credit, which is used for determining 
  2066  standing on the retention register. OPM did not receive significant

  2089  B. Part 351, Subpart C: Changes in Transfer of Function Procedures

  2091      OPM is substituting the word ``agency'' for ``competitive area'' 
  2092  throughout subpart C and making other conforming changes, so as to 
  2093  align with the text of the statute Congress enacted governing transfers 
  2094  of functions (5 U.S.C. 3503), which applies to transfers of functions 
  2095  between agencies, not within agencies. Notably, the regulations 
  2096  governing transfers of function applicable to the SES apply only to 
  2097  ``the transfer of the performance of a continuing function from one 
  2098  agency to one or more other agencies.'' 5 CFR 359.608 (emphasis added); 
  2099  see also 5 U.S.C. 3595 (providing to the SES rights comparable to those 
  2100  provided by 5 U.S.C. 3503). Similarly, OPM's regulations in Sec.  
  2101  353.109 regarding restoration to duty from uniformed service or 
  2102  compensable injury only speak of transfers between agencies.

  2104  provide advance notice and the opportunity to follow one's function 
  2105  when functions are transferred between competitive areas within a 
  2106  single agency, even if the full transfer-of-function procedures of 
  2107  Subpart C are not required.'' OPM disagrees. It believes that agencies 
  2108  will appropriately seek to retain talented and knowledgeable employees 
  2109  during intra-agency transfers of function even without a regulatory 
  2110  requirement to provide advance notice and the opportunity to transfer 
  2111  when a function is transferred within a single agency. OPM believes

  2113  carrying out internal restructurings and generates litigation without a

  2122  must use the adverse action procedures found in 5 CFR part 752, if 
  2123  applicable, or other procedures required by law, regulation, or the 
  2124  terms of the employee's appointment, if it chooses to separate a 
  2125  competing employee who declines to transfer with his or her function. 
  2126  That is because some employees affected by transfer-of-function 
  2127  procedures may not be covered by part 752, and some separations may be

  2129      OPM is revising Sec.  351.302(g) to clarify the procedures that

  2132  is also revising Sec.  351.303 to simplify the process for identifying

  2253  D. Part 351, Subpart E: New Method of Deriving Retention Standing, 
  2254  Revised Order of Retention Examples, and Additional Examples
  2255  
  2256      OPM is finalizing its changes to 5 CFR part 351, subpart E 
  2257  ``Retention Standing,'' including revised and reorganized content in 
  2258  Sec. Sec.  351.501 through 351.504. In addition, OPM is renumbering 
  2259  current Sec.  351.505 Records and Sec.  351.506 Effective date of 
  2260  retention standing to Sec.  351.506 Records and Sec.  351.507 Effective 
  2261  date of retention standing, respectively.
  2262      As noted above, under this rule (and particularly Sec.  351.501 
  2263  Order of retention), when determining the order in which employees are 
  2264  placed on a RIF retention register, agencies will now do so based on 
  2265  whether the employee is in the competitive service tenure group or 
  2266  excepted service tenure group. Within each group, employees will be 
  2267  ranked based on performance, as augmented by additional points for 
  2268  veterans' preference. Where employees are tied, the employee in the 
  2269  higher tenure subgroup (with subgroup I ranked ahead of subgroup II) 
  2270  will be ranked ahead. When employees are still tied, the employee with 
  2271  the longer service will be ranked ahead.
  2272      In Sec.  351.502 Tenure of employment, OPM is redefining the tenure 
  2273  groups for both the competitive and excepted services. The competitive 
  2274  service tenure group will consist of all competitive service employees 
  2275  (in accordance with the provisions of Sec.  315.201) who are not (as of 
  2276  the date of the RIF notice) serving an initial probationary period or a 
  2277  temporary or time-limited appointment of 1 year or less under 5 CFR 
  2278  part 316. The excepted service tenure group will consist of excepted 
  2279  service employees occupying a career position (as defined in Sec.  
  2280  213.101) who are not serving a trial period and are not serving in a 
  2281  temporary or time-limited appointment of 1 year or less.
  2282      In addition, competitive service tenure subgroup I will include 
  2283  each career employee in the competitive service who, as of the date the 
  2284  employee receives a specific reduction in force notice, is not serving 
  2285  an initial probationary period. This definition is substantially the 
  2286  same as the current competitive service tenure group I.
  2287      Competitive service tenure subgroup II will consist of every other 
  2288  competitive service employee who, as of the date of the RIF notice, is 
  2289  not serving an initial probationary period or a temporary or term 
  2290  appointment of 1 year or less. For example, an employee serving under a 
  2291  career-conditional competitive service appointment who has completed a 
  2292  probationary period but not yet completed the service requirements for 
  2293  career tenure (under 5 CFR 315.201) would be included in subgroup II.
  2294      Excepted service tenure subgroup I will include all employees 
  2295  occupying a career position (that is to say, not in Schedule C or G) in 
  2296  the excepted service who, as of the date the employee receives a 
  2297  specific reduction in force notice, are not serving a trial period and 
  2298  whose appointment carries no restriction or condition such as 
  2299  conditional, indefinite, or specific time limit. This definition is 
  2300  substantially the same as current excepted service tenure group I.
  2301      Excepted service tenure subgroup II will consist of all other 
  2302  career employees in the excepted service (that is to say, not in 
  2303  Schedule C or G) who are not serving a trial period or a temporary or 
  2304  time-limited appointment of 1 year or less. Examples of employees in 
  2305  excepted service tenure subgroup II include employees occupying career 
  2306  positions in the excepted service who have completed any required trial 
  2307  period and who are serving under conditional, indefinite, or specific 
  2308  time-limited appointments of more than 1 year.

  2438      New paragraph Sec.  351.503(e) Multiple rating patterns addresses 
  2439  situations in which an agency has employees in a competitive area who 
  2440  have ratings of record under more than one pattern of summary levels, 
  2441  as described in 5 CFR 430.208(e). An agency may, in its sole and 
  2442  exclusive discretion, choose to provide enhanced performance credit to 
  2443  employees under disparate pattern summary levels. It may do so by 
  2444  transmuting or assigning an employee a higher summary level rating than 
  2445  what he or she received under a previous rating system when there is 
  2446  documented evidence of exceptional or higher-level performance 
  2447  consistent with the criteria in revised Sec.  351.503(d).
  2448      In addition, for an employee who goes from an appraisal system 
  2449  which uses a higher pattern of summary levels to a lower one (e.g., an 
  2450  employee who goes from a 5 summary level appraisal program to a two 
  2451  level system (i.e., pass/fail system)), an agency may adopt policies 
  2452  which would allow employees with ratings above the highest summary 
  2453  level of the lower pattern system to be listed ahead of any employee on 
  2454  the retention register who does not have documented evidence of 
  2455  exceptional performance as described above. This method allows agencies 
  2456  to adopt policies that would prevent exceptional performers from being 
  2457  disadvantaged because they may be covered under two or more patterns of 
  2458  summary rating levels which may not make meaningful distinctions for 
  2459  performance among employees. Further, Sec.  351.503 will require RIF 
  2460  performance ratings and assigned summary levels, including adjustments, 
  2461  to be uniformly and consistently applied within the competitive area 
  2462  and consistent with the agency's implementing issuances. Where an 
  2463  agency elects to assign additional performance credit, the agency must 
  2464  specify and document the criteria in advance and make them available 
  2465  for review.
  2466      Paragraph (f) of Sec.  351.503 describes how an agency should 
  2467  factor performance ratings into the RIF process when an employee does 
  2468  not have three actual ratings of record during the 4-year period prior 
  2469  to the date of issuance of RIF notices, or the 4-year period prior to 
  2470  the agency-established cut-off date. It uses the modal rating concept 
  2471  for employees with no ratings during the 4-year period prior to the 
  2472  RIF, as currently found in Sec.  351.504(c)(1), but modifies the 
  2473  current provisions by removing the reference to ``additional retention 
  2474  service credit.''

  2476  preference will be applied in a RIF in both the competitive and 
  2477  excepted services. Each preference eligible employee with a compensable 
  2478  service-connected disability of 30 percent or more will receive an 
  2479  additional 5 points added to their performance credit, while every 
  2480  other preference eligible employee will receive an additional 3 points 
  2481  added to their performance credit. ``Preference eligibles'' is defined 
  2482  in 5 U.S.C. 2108(3) to include not only veterans, but also certain 
  2483  close family members of deceased or service-disabled veterans. Non-

  2487  ``the proposed rules are vague and unclear as to exactly how 
  2488  performance and veterans' issues are to be determined,'' but does not

  2491  contended that ``[t]he proposed regulation will make it likely that the 
  2492  classifications will result in numerous appeals challenging the order 
  2493  and create chaos in their implementation as a result,'' but failed to 
  2494  explain how the new regulation is more complicated than the current 
  2495  rules.
  2496      OPM disagrees with Commenter 0660's assertions. The current rules 
  2497  require agencies to categorize employees based on tenure group and 
  2498  veterans' preference subgroup. Employees are ranked first by tenure 
  2499  group I, II, III; then within each tenure group by veterans' preference 
  2500  subgroup AD, A, B; and only then by years of service as augmented by 
  2501  performance credit, starting with the earliest service date. Agencies 
  2502  then prepare an ``adjusted SCD'' calculation where extra years of 
  2503  service are added to an employee's actual service computation date. 
  2504  That means current RIF ordering is not a simple comparison of Employee 
  2505  A's performance against Employee B's performance. Agencies must first 
  2506  place employees into tenure groups, then veterans' preference 
  2507  subgroups, then calculate adjusted service dates. Performance affects 
  2508  ranking only inside the employee's already-determined tenure/veterans' 
  2509  preference category.
  2510      Agencies then must undergo multiple rounds of complicated bumping 
  2511  and retreating before arriving at a final retention register. Notably, 
  2512  ``bump and retreat'' can create a chain. If Employee A bumps Employee 
  2513  B, then Employee B is released from that competitive level, and the 
  2514  agency must determine whether Employee B has his or her own bump or 
  2515  retreat right. This process is highly burdensome and prone to errors.
  2516      This rule replaces the current rules with a streamlined system that 
  2517  eliminates the need for multiple, complicated rounds of bump and 
  2518  retreat, replacing it with a straightforward comparison of employee 
  2519  performance as augmented by veterans' preference, with ties broken by 
  2520  tenure and length of service. Further, OPM's new rules are simpler 
  2521  because they eliminate the most confusing features of the current 
  2522  rules: using performance to manufacture an adjusted service computation 
  2523  date and complicated bump-and-retreat procedures.
  2524      This rule addresses that problem by making performance credit more 
  2525  transparent and direct: Level 5 ratings receive 7 points, Level 4 
  2526  ratings receive 5 points, Level 3 ratings receive 3 points, and Level 1 
  2527  or 2 ratings receive no points. Veterans' preference is then added to 
  2528  that performance credit.
  2529      This rule's use of defined point values--Level 5 = 7 points, Level 
  2530  4 = 5 points, Level 3 = 3 points, and Level 1 or 2 = 0 points--also 
  2531  makes the RIF calculation easier to understand and audit than an 
  2532  artificial performance-adjusted SCD. As Commenter 0687 noted, this 
  2533  reform simplifies the composition of retention registers.
  2534      In addition, this rule does not change the basic record-keeping 
  2535  requirements in current Sec.  351.505 (renumbered to Sec.  351.506) or 
  2536  the notice requirements in Sec.  351.802, except to conform their 
  2537  provisions to other changes made in this rulemaking. Thus, OPM does not 
  2538  agree with Commenter 0678's assertion that the rule ``reduces notice 
  2539  and transparency'' regarding RIFs. Instead, OPM agrees with Commenter 
  2540  0687, who noted that the revisions ``simplify[ ] the composition of 
  2541  retention registers . . . such that retention standing is faster to 
  2542  compute, more transparent, and more equitably applied.''
  2543  
  2544  [[Page 49199]]
  2545  
  2546      In the proposed rule, OPM provided order of retention examples. 
  2547  Commenter 0680 points out correctly that some of the tables 
  2548  illustrating the operation of the proposed rule contained errors, as 
  2549  they incorrectly ranked employees in a higher tenure subgroup ahead of 
  2550  employees with a greater performance credit. OPM is therefore 
  2551  correcting these examples below. OPM is also publishing further 
  2552  examples of how retention standing will work under the new regulations 
  2553  to aid with administration of the new rules.
  2554      OPM disagrees with Commenter 0680 that these inadvertent errors 
  2555  show a lack of reasoned decision-making, that the new rules increase 
  2556  the risk of mistakes, or that OPM or agencies are unprepared to 
  2557  administer the new rules. Such a correction is consistent with ordinary 
  2558  rulemaking practice: agencies often revise, add, delete, or correct 
  2559  examples to conform them to the operative regulatory standard or to 
  2560  respond to comments.\16\ The binding rule is the regulatory text, which 
  2561  provides that employees are ranked by performance credit as augmented 
  2562  by veterans' preference, with tenure subgroup and service computation 
  2563  date used as tie-breakers. The proposed rule text clearly stated that, 
  2564  within each tenure group, employees are ranked by performance credit as 
  2565  augmented by veterans' preference, and only when employees have the 
  2566  same augmented performance credit are they further ranked by tenure 
  2567  subgroup and then by length of service.
  2568      Indeed, OPM believes the new RIF formula is much simpler to 
  2569  understand and apply than the current formula, as it involves a simple 
  2570  calculation of performance credits adjusted for veterans' status, with 
  2571  tenure subgroup and length of service serving as tiebreakers. The 
  2572  current system, by contrast, involves a multi-layered system where 
  2573  employees were sorted into three tenure groups, with veterans' status 
  2574  subgroups within each tenure group, with employees then further sorted 
  2575  by service computation date that is adjusted based on performance. That 
  2576  process required agencies to translate performance into years, average 
  2577  the credited years, round where necessary, and then move the employee's 
  2578  service date backward to create an ``adjusted SCD.'' That made the 
  2579  register harder to understand because the service computation date was 
  2580  not the employee's actual service date, but an artificial service date 
  2581  reflecting both service and performance. Further, agencies were then 
  2582  required to engage in complicated ``bump and retreat'' exercises 
  2583  between employees in different tenure groups, often encompassing 
  2584  multiple rounds of RIF competition governed by detailed rules that were 
  2585  understood by very few beyond a very small group of Federal HR 
  2586  specialists and consultants.
  2587      Under this rule, by contrast, performance remains a score that 
  2588  corresponds to direct numerical values, augmented by consistent 
  2589  numerical values for veterans' preference. Thus, the new rules will 
  2590  likely result in far fewer errors than the old rules. They are also 
  2591  easier and more streamlined, making them easier to apply and understand 
  2592  by both HR offices and Federal employees. Employees who inspect the 
  2593  register will be much more likely to understand how their retention 
  2594  standing was calculated and be able to spot errors.
  2595      Several commenters agree that the new regulations are simpler than 
  2596  the current ones. Commenter 0687 noted that the new rule simplifies the 
  2597  composition of retention registers and the application of assignment 
  2598  rights, versus the current complicated ``bump and retreat'' process.

  2600  rules are ``substantial and should not be understated,'' and that ``the 
  2601  proposal's effort to simplify the RIF framework represents a meaningful 
  2602  and constructive reform.''

  2807      OPM is modifying Sec.  351.506(c) to make these provisions

  2810  OPM is also clarifying Sec.  351.506(d) that employees who have not 
  2811  received specific RIF notices may have rights to review retention 
  2812  registers and related records under other laws such as the Freedom of 
  2813  Information Act (FOIA).
  2814      OPM is revising Sec.  351.507 to make clear that the effective date 
  2815  of retention standing is measured as of the date the employee receives 
  2816  a specific reduction in force notice, not the date a RIF separation 
  2817  actually occurs. Commenters did not express significant concerns 
  2818  regarding this change, which will make it more administratively 
  2819  feasible for agencies to conduct a RIF in instances where the actual 
  2820  date of RIF separation is delayed due to litigation or other unforeseen 
  2821  factors. This change also addresses concerns expressed by some 
  2822  commenters (like Commenter 0449) that agencies might change performance 
  2823  ratings between announcement and execution of a RIF.
  2824      OPM is making additional changes to Sec.  351.805(b), New notice 
  2825  required, to conform with the changes to Sec.  351.507 and confirm that 
  2826  an amended notice issued solely to state a later effective date is not 
  2827  a new specific reduction in force notice for purposes of Sec.  351.507 
  2828  and does not require the agency to redetermine or recalculate retention 
  2829  standing under subpart E. This amendment affirms the necessary 
  2830  consequence of the changes to Sec.  351.507: once retention standing is 
  2831  fixed as of the date of the specific RIF notice, a ministerial amended 
  2832  notice delaying the effective date does not restart the retention-

  2835  E. Part 351, Subpart F: Furloughs, Abolishment of Competitive Area, 
  2836  USERRA Rights, and Exceptions
  2837  
  2838      OPM is modifying Sec.  351.601 for consistency with how retention 
  2839  standing is to be calculated under Subpart E of part 351. OPM is also 
  2840  modifying Sec.  351.602 to remove the prohibition on retaining an 
  2841  employee serving a specifically limited temporary appointment in a 
  2842  competitive level while releasing a competing employee from that level. 
  2843  OPM did not receive significant adverse comments on these provisions 
  2844  and is finalizing them.
  2845  1. RIF Furloughs
  2846      In the proposed rule, OPM proposed to modify its regulations in 
  2847  Sec.  351.604 regarding furloughs of more than 30 consecutive calendar 
  2848  days (or more than 22 workdays if done on a discontinuous basis over a 
  2849  period not exceeding 1 year) to remove the requirement that agencies 
  2850  furlough employees based on retention standing and recall employees to 
  2851  duty from furlough based on retention standing.
  2852      Commenter 0687 opposed these changes, contending that they had ``no 
  2853  obvious use case and could create mechanisms for abuse.'' Commenter 
  2854  0687 noted that agencies typically do not engage in unpaid furloughs of 
  2855  any length, whether greater or less than 30 days, and that OPM's 
  2856  proposed revision would create risks that agencies could use long 
  2857  furloughs to circumvent normal RIF procedures. Commenter 0687 therefore 
  2858  contended that the risks of this new provision outweigh the benefits. 
  2859  Commenter 0117 similarly expressed concern that agencies could use 
  2860  long-term unpaid furloughs to avoid following retention order 
  2861  requirements. OPM agrees that its proposed changes to Sec.  351.604 
  2862  warrant further consideration and has chosen not to finalize them.
  2863  2. Abolishment of a Competitive Area
  2864      In this rule, OPM is renaming Sec.  351.605 as Abolishment of a 
  2865  competitive area to more accurately describe its purpose. The revised 
  2866  section explains that the appropriate use of this provision is when an 
  2867  agency is abolishing all positions (including the positions of 
  2868  employees otherwise excluded from RIF competition under Sec.  
  2869  351.202(d)) in a competitive area within 180 days. It further explains 
  2870  that, because all positions in the competitive area will be eliminated, 
  2871  an agency is not required to release competing employees in order of 
  2872  retention standing.
  2873      As the D.C. Circuit explained in upholding an earlier version of 
  2874  this provision, when all employees in a competitive area will be 
  2875  released within a relatively short time, ``it is certainly reasonable 
  2876  to conclude that it would be a waste of resources for an agency to be 
  2877  forced to perform detailed seniority and performance calculations 
  2878  solely to construct a rank ordering of employees' retention rights when

  3052      OPM is revising Sec.  351.701(a) to replace tenure groups I and II

  3207  I. Part 330: RPL, ICTAP, and CTAP
  3208  
  3209      OPM is making various changes to 5 CFR part 330 to conform the 
  3210  provisions of this part pertaining to RPL, ICTAP, and CTAP to the other 
  3211  changes made in this rulemaking, most notably the modifications to 
  3212  tenure groups I, II and III, and to update some of the terminology. 
  3213  RPL, ICTAP, and CTAP are designed to help employees who have been, or 
  3214  are about to be, displaced by a RIF find continued Federal employment, 
  3215  so part 330 needs to align with the revised RIF definitions and 
  3216  concepts in part 351. In the proposed rule, OPM stated expressly that 
  3217  it does not intend for the coverage definitions to apply retroactively

  3219  separation notice, declined a directed geographic reassignment, or

  3226  definition of ``qualified'' in Sec.  330.202 to align with OPM's 
  3227  definition of that same term in Sec.  351.702 (in the context of 
  3228  assignment rights in a RIF). To be qualified for a position, an RPL 
  3229  registrant, just like an employee competing in a RIF, will be required 
  3230  to have the capacity, adaptability, and special skills necessary to 
  3231  satisfactorily perform the duties of the position, as demonstrated 
  3232  through a valid, job-related assessment. This change strengthens RPL 
  3233  placement by ensuring candidates are matched to jobs through real, job-

  3237  for selecting qualified RPL placement priority candidates based on 
  3238  numerical scoring. Instead of rating and ranking candidates based on 
  3239  job experience and education, an agency using this method must instead 
  3240  rate and rank candidates based on their job-related skills, knowledge, 
  3241  and competencies as measured by an assessment. Agencies using the 
  3242  numerical scoring method will be required to rate and rank qualified 
  3243  RPL placement priority candidates in a fair and consistent manner, and 
  3244  will be required to assign additional points to candidates based on 
  3245  veterans' preference. This change maintains RPL priority but makes the 
  3246  selection process more skills-based and consistent with the revised RIF 
  3247  framework.

  3249  part 330. It noted that the frameworks governing RPL, CTAP and ICTAP 
  3250  were developed decades ago, and the changes proposed by OPM would align 
  3251  these programs with the performance-forward retention model, improve 
  3252  clarity around eligibility and priority placement, and support more

  3303  restoration protections for employees absent because of uniformed 
  3304  service or compensable injury operate coherently with the final 
  3305  revisions to part 351.
  3306      Current Sec.  353.209(a) already provides that an employee 
  3307  performing duty with the uniformed services may not be demoted or 
  3308  separated, other than military separation, except for cause; that RIF 
  3309  is not ``for cause''; that such an employee is not a competing employee 
  3310  under part 351; and that, if the employee's position is abolished 
  3311  during the absence, the agency must reassign the employee to another 
  3312  position of like status and pay. This final rule clarifies that this 
  3313  reassignment obligation applies when the employee's position is 
  3314  abolished as part of the abolishment of an entire competitive area 
  3315  under Sec.  351.605. These additional edits clarify how restoration 
  3316  rights apply when an employee's position is abolished in connection 
  3317  with a RIF, including when an agency abolishes all positions in a 
  3318  competitive area under Sec.  351.605.
  3319      OPM is removing a reference to tenure group III in Sec.  
  3320  353.301(a). Instead of ``tenure group III,'' OPM is substituting 
  3321  ``temporary, term or indefinite appointment,'' which encompasses the 
  3322  categories previously included in tenure group III.

  3324  K. Part 359: SES Furloughs
  3325  
  3326      Consistent with the changes to the definition of ``furlough'' in 
  3327  Sec.  351.203, OPM is revising the definition of ``furlough'' in Sec.  
  3328  359.802 (regulating furloughs in the SES) to align with OPM's

  3331  appropriations where the ultimate duration of the furlough is unknown 
  3332  at the outset. Commenter 0683 agreed that this change appropriately 
  3333  distinguishes between planned agency-initiated furloughs and emergency 
  3334  furloughs driven by congressional inaction. OPM did not receive 
  3335  significant adverse comment regarding this change and is finalizing it.
  3336  
  3337  L. Part 362: Pathways Programs
  3338  
  3339      OPM is modifying 5 CFR 362.205 regarding the Pathways Intern 
  3340  Program by removing references to how RIF procedures apply to Pathways 
  3341  interns, as those references would no longer be accurate or necessary 
  3342  given OPM's changes to Part 351. Pursuant to revised Sec.  351.502(b), 
  3343  the termination of a Pathways intern will only be covered by RIF 
  3344  procedures if the intern had completed a trial period under 5 CFR 11.3. 
  3345  Otherwise, Pathways interns could be retained or separated by an agency 
  3346  without regard to RIF procedures.

  3348  Graduates Program regulation to the final revisions to part 351. 
  3349  Current Sec.  362.306(a) provides that Recent Graduates are in excepted 
  3350  service Tenure Group II for purposes of Sec.  351.502 and that 
  3351  expiration of a Recent Graduates appointment is not otherwise subject 
  3352  to part 351. Because this final rule replaces the prior excepted-
  3353  service tenure-group structure with the ``excepted service tenure 
  3354  group'' and excludes employees serving a trial period from RIF 
  3355  competition, the current reference to excepted service Tenure Group II 
  3356  is no longer accurate.

  3358  excepted service tenure group for purposes of Sec.  351.502 upon 
  3359  completion of a trial period under Sec.  11.3. This amendment 
  3360  harmonizes Sec.  362.306 with the revised definition of ``competing 
  3361  employee'' and the revised coverage and tenure provisions in part 351. 
  3362  It also parallels the rule's treatment of Pathways interns, for whom 
  3363  OPM proposed to remove obsolete RIF language because Pathways 
  3364  participants serving trial periods are not competing employees under 
  3365  the revised part 351 framework. Revising Sec.  362.306(a) applies the 
  3366  same principle to the Recent Graduates Program and prevents confusion 
  3367  caused by obsolete tenure-group terminology.

  3373  430.208 refers to summary levels as a reference point for assigning 
  3374  additional retention service credit under part 351. Because this rule

  3380  ratings of record and applying related regulations. Thus, ratings of

  3386      Enhanced performance values under Sec.  351.503 do not change the

    93  I. Executive Summary
    94  
    95      OPM is revising its regulations governing RIFs and making related 
    96  changes to its regulations under statutory authority found at 5 U.S.C. 
    97  1103, 1104, 1302, 3304, 3320, 3330, 3502, 3503, 3596, 4305, and 4315, 
    98  and 38 U.S.C. 4331. The rule makes the following changes:
    99      1. Replaces the current tenure-group framework with a simplified 
   100  competitive service and excepted service structure. The rule 
   101  consolidates current tenure groups I, II, and III into a ``competitive 
   102  service tenure group'' and an ``excepted service tenure group,'' with 
   103  two subgroups in each.
   104      2. Excludes certain employees from RIF competition. Employees 
   105  serving initial probationary periods, trial periods, temporary or time-
   106  limited appointments of one year or less, and Schedule C and Schedule G 
   107  employees are not ``competing employees'' for RIF purposes and can be 
   108  retained, furloughed, separated, demoted, or reassigned without using 
   109  RIF procedures.
   110      3. Reorders retention standing to place performance first. Agencies 
   111  will maintain separate retention registers for competitive service and 
   112  excepted service employees; within each group, employees will be ranked 
   113  by performance credit, augmented by veterans' preference, with tenure 
   114  subgroup and length of service used as tie-breakers.
   115      4. Creates a new numerical performance credit methodology. Agencies 
   116  will calculate performance credit using the three most recent ratings 
   117  of record from the relevant four-year period, assigning 7 points for 
   118  Level 5, 5 points for Level 4, 3 points for Level 3, and 0 points for 
   119  Level 1 or Level 2 ratings, with special rules for missing ratings and 
   120  differing appraisal patterns.
   121      5. Applies veterans' preference by adding points to performance 
   122  credit. Preference eligibles with a compensable service-connected 
   123  disability of 30 percent or more receive 5 additional points; other 
   124  preference eligibles receive 3 additional points; non-preference 
   125  eligibles receive no additional points.
   126      6. Adds definitions of key terms. The rule defines ``competing 
   127  employee,'' ``competitive service tenure group,'' ``excepted service 
   128  tenure group,'' ``reduction in force,'' ``initial probationary 
   129  period,'' ``trial period,'' ``government obligation,'' and ``military 
   130  spouse.''
   131      7. Excludes emergency shutdown furloughs from the RIF furlough 
   132  definition. The rule excludes emergency shutdown furloughs caused by 
   133  lapses in appropriations from the RIF furlough definition.
   134      8. Removes erosion of duties reclassifications from actions 
   135  requiring RIF procedures, while adding an anti-manipulation safeguard. 
   136  Agencies will no longer need to use RIF procedures for such 
   137  reclassifications but could not undertake an erosion of duties 
   138  reclassification after announcing a RIF if it would adversely affect an 
   139  employee's retention standing.
   140      9. Narrows and simplifies transfer-of-function requirements. The 
   141  rule narrows transfer-of-function requirements to transfers between 
   142  agencies, rather than transfers within a single agency, and simplifies 
   143  identification of employees tied to a transferring function by focusing 
   144  on whether the employee performs the function at least half of the 
   145  time.
   146      10. Clarifies how agencies define competitive areas. Under this 
   147  rule, competitive areas may be based on official organizational units 
   148  or combinations of units. Agencies may define certain geographic 
   149  locations as separate competitive areas, while employees working at 
   150  approved alternate locations remain assigned to their official 
   151  organizational unit for competitive area purposes. In addition, an 
   152  organizational unit for RIF purposes must be clearly distinguished from 
   153  other organizational units with regard to its operation, work function, 
   154  staff, and supervisory oversight.
   155      11. Clarifies and simplifies procedures when an entire competitive 
   156  area is being abolished. When abolishing all positions in a competitive 
   157  area within 180 days, agencies may release employees without ranking 
   158  them on a retention register or applying assignment rights, and with a 
   159  simplified notice.
   160      12. Revises and simplifies assignment rights by replacing ``bump 
   161  and retreat'' concepts with assignment rights to a position held by an 
   162  employee with a lower-retention-standing. A released employee in the 
   163  competitive service will receive assignment rights to a qualifying 
   164  position held by another employee with lower retention standing in the 
   165  same tenure group, generally within three grades below the released 
   166  employee's position, or five grades for certain 30-percent-or-more 
   167  disabled veterans.
   168      13. Requires skills-based assessments for RIF assignment 
   169  qualifications and RPL selection. Agencies must assess whether 
   170  employees or RPL candidates have the capacity, adaptability, and skills 
   171  needed for the position through job-related assessments based on job 
   172  analysis (unless the employee held the same or substantially similar 
   173  position within five years of the RIF and achieved a rating of Level 3 
   174  (Fully Successful), or higher, or equivalent, for performing the duties 
   175  of the position). This change requires agencies to use more rigorous 
   176  assessments in accordance with the Chance to Compete Act of 2024 (Pub. 
   177  L. 118-188) to determine whether the individual is qualified.
   178      14. Updates RPL, CTAP and ICTAP rules to conform to the new RIF 
   179  framework. The rule replaces references to prior tenure groups with the 
   180  new competitive service tenure group, preserves preexisting eligibility 
   181  through OPM-recognized qualifying appointments, updates selection 
   182  methods to emphasize skills-based assessments, and adds exceptions 
   183  allowing agencies to retain or finalize appointments of probationary 
   184  employees.
   185  
   186  [[Page 49179]]
   187  
   188      15. Updates Pathways and post-secondary student regulations to 
   189  conform to the new RIF framework. The rule modifies regulations in 5 
   190  CFR parts 316 and 362, pertaining to post-secondary students and 
   191  Pathways Programs, to clarify how such appointments are treated for RIF 
   192  purposes in conformance with the changes made by this rule.
   193      16. Revises RIF exceptions, notices, and records, and makes various 
   194  conforming changes in other regulatory sections. The rule clarifies 
   195  continuing and temporary exceptions allowing agencies to retain 
   196  employees who would otherwise be separated via a RIF, including for 
   197  government obligations, parental leave, sick-leave-related 
   198  circumstances, annual leave, and military spouses; fixes retention 
   199  standing as of the date the employee receives a specific RIF notice 
   200  (rather than the date the RIF is executed); updates required notice 
   201  content; and makes conforming changes for post-secondary students, 
   202  Pathways interns, compensable-injury restoration rights, Senior 
   203  Executive Service (SES) furloughs, and performance management cross-
   204  references.
   205      In addition, in this rule, OPM is modifying the proposed rule in 
   206  the following ways:
   207      1. Clarifying how retention and restoration rights under the 
   208  Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act of 1994 
   209  (USERRA) apply in a RIF. In response to public comments, this rule 
   210  provides additional clarity regarding how USERRA applies to RIFs. It 
   211  requires that agencies apply USERRA retention protections and 
   212  restoration rights as a mandatory exception to the order of release 
   213  under a RIF. When an entire competitive area is abolished pursuant to 
   214  Sec.  351.605, an employee entitled to USERRA retention protections or 
   215  restoration rights must be assigned to a different position at the 
   216  agency. If an entire agency is abolished, OPM will provide placement 
   217  assistance elsewhere in the Executive Branch.
   218      2. Reinforcing Merit System Principles. OPM is revising Sec.  
   219  351.204 to clarify that agencies have a responsibility not only to 
   220  follow and apply the regulations in Part 351 when conducting a RIF, but 
   221  to ensure that the RIF regulations are administered and applied 
   222  consistent with all applicable laws, including the merit system 
   223  principles set forth in 5 U.S.C. 2301(b).
   224      3. Providing additional competitive area safeguards. OPM is 
   225  requiring that, when a competitive area will be in effect less than 90 
   226  days prior to a specific RIF notice, or has been materially modified, 
   227  an agency must submit a description of the competitive area and 
   228  provide, for OPM review, a written explanation of the bona fide 
   229  organizational basis for the competitive area.
   230      4. Clarifying exclusions of employees from RIF competition in Sec.  
   231  351.202(d). The final rule clarifies that if the individuals among the 
   232  categories of employees specified in Sec.  351.202(d) as excluded from 
   233  RIF competition are released for the reasons described in Sec.  
   234  351.201(a)(2) (i.e., lack of work, shortage of funds, insufficient 
   235  personnel ceiling, reorganization, or the exercise of reemployment 
   236  rights or restoration rights), they must receive a modified RIF notice, 
   237  unless the release is the natural expiration of the temporary or time-
   238  limited appointment.
   239      5. Making various clarifying and conforming changes and updating an 
   240  outdated reference. The final rule makes changes to the wording of 
   241  Sec.  351.605, dealing with abolishment of a competitive area, to 
   242  further clarify the meaning of this provision; makes minor changes to 
   243  the definition of ``emergency shutdown furlough'' in Sec.  351.203 and 
   244  Sec.  359.802 to remove potentially confusing language; updates Sec.  
   245  353.110 to replace outdated OPM contact information for placement 
   246  assistance; adds an introductory phrase to Sec.  351.802(a); and makes 
   247  conforming changes to Sec.  351.805, dealing with successive RIF 
   248  notices, and Sec.  362.306, dealing with Pathways recent graduates, to 
   249  ensure consistency with other changes made in this rulemaking.
   250      6. Not finalizing changes to RIF furlough procedures. In response 
   251  to input from public comments, OPM has elected not to finalize a 
   252  further change to provide greater flexibility for agencies to conduct 
   253  unpaid furloughs of more than 30 days.
   254

   256
